exemplars.name: String vs StringBuilder
exemplars.question: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer in Java?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand immutability and its implications, when mutation matters for performance, and whether you know that StringBuffer's synchronization is rarely needed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recommending StringBuffer for thread-safety without realizing that compound operations (append + append) still aren't atomic, or not knowing that the compiler converts simple string concatenation to StringBuilder internally
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the Java compiler rewrites `+` concatenation to StringBuilder for single-expression concatenation, but a loop with `+` still creates O(n) intermediate Strings. Mention Java 15+ text blocks and that Java 9+ uses StringConcatFactory for even better inlining.

sections.title: The Core Trade-off
sections.content:
All three classes represent sequences of characters, but they differ fundamentally in how they handle modification. **String** is backed by a `final byte[]` (since Java 9; previously `char[]`) that cannot be changed after construction — every "modification" method like `concat()`, `replace()`, or `substring()` allocates a new String and copies the relevant characters. This makes String inherently thread-safe and hashable, but expensive when you need to build strings iteratively.

**StringBuilder** and **StringBuffer** both extend `AbstractStringBuilder`, which maintains a **mutable** `byte[]` buffer with a separate length counter. When you call `append()`, it writes into the existing buffer (growing it by doubling when necessary), avoiding the allocation-per-modification cost. The only difference between them is synchronization: StringBuffer wraps every method in `synchronized`, while StringBuilder does not. Since most string building is single-threaded (building a response, formatting a log line, constructing a query), StringBuilder's lack of synchronization makes it the standard choice.

sections.title: Feature Comparison
sections.content:
| Feature | String | StringBuilder | StringBuffer |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mutable | ❌ Immutable | ✅ Mutable | ✅ Mutable |
| Thread-safe | ✅ (immutable = safe) | ❌ Not synchronized | ✅ Methods synchronized |
| Performance (single thread) | ⚠️ Creates new object per change | ✅ Fastest | ⚠️ Slower (lock overhead) |
| String pool / interning | ✅ Literals are pooled | ❌ Not pooled | ❌ Not pooled |
| Use case | Constants, keys, labels | String building in a loop | Legacy APIs; rarely needed |

sections.title: The Performance Trap: String Concatenation in Loops
String Pool and Immutability Implications
sections.content:
String literals like `"hello"` are stored in the **String pool** — a JVM-level deduplication cache. Two literals with the same content share the same object: `"hello" == "hello"` is `true`. This works because String is immutable — sharing is safe when no one can modify the shared value.

`new String("hello")` always creates a new object, bypassing the pool — which is why `new String("hello") == "hello"` is `false` but `.equals()` is `true`. You can force pooling with `.intern()`, but this is rarely needed in modern Java.

Immutability also makes String safe as a **HashMap key** — if the key could be mutated after insertion, the hash would change and the entry would be lost in the wrong bucket. And it makes String inherently **thread-safe** — no synchronization needed because no thread can change the value.

StringBuilder and StringBuffer are never pooled, never safe as map keys, and StringBuilder is not thread-safe (though StringBuffer's per-method synchronization is misleading — `buffer.append(a).append(b)` is two separate locks, not one atomic operation).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **String is immutable** — `s.concat("x")` returns a new object, the original `s` is unchanged. This makes String thread-safe, usable as a HashMap key, and eligible for the JVM's String pool (`"hello" == "hello"` is `true`)
- **StringBuilder** is mutable — `sb.append("x")` modifies the internal `char[]` in place, no new objects. Use it inside loops: `for(...)  { sb.append(row); }` avoids O(n) intermediate String allocations
- **StringBuffer** = StringBuilder + `synchronized` on every method — but `buffer.append(x).append(y)` is two separate locks, so another thread can interleave between them. Almost never the right choice
- **Compiler handles single expressions** — `"Hello, " + name + "!"` is auto-rewritten to StringBuilder (or `StringConcatFactory` on Java 9+). You only need manual StringBuilder inside **loops**
- **String pool tip** — `new String("hello")` creates a new object bypassing the pool; `"hello"` and `"hello".intern()` are pooled. StringBuilder/StringBuffer are never pooled

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The core difference is **mutability**. String is immutable — every method that looks like it modifies a String actually returns a brand-new object. `s.toUpperCase()` doesn't change `s` — it creates a new String. That immutability is what makes String safe to share across threads, safe to use as a HashMap key, and eligible for the JVM's **string pool** — the deduplication cache where `"hello" == "hello"` is literally `true`.

The problem shows up in **loops**. If you write `result += column` inside a loop, each iteration creates a new String — that's O(n) allocations and O(n²) total copying. **StringBuilder** fixes this: `sb.append(column)` modifies an internal `char[]` buffer in place — amortized O(1), no new objects until you call `toString()`.

**StringBuffer** is the legacy twin — identical API, but every method is `synchronized`. The trap is that synchronization on individual methods doesn't make compound operations atomic. `buffer.append(x).append(y)` is two separate locks — another thread can interleave between them. You get locking overhead without real atomicity. In modern code, StringBuffer is essentially never the right answer.

One thing worth mentioning: the **compiler is smarter than people think**. For a single expression like `"Hello, " + name + "!"`, it already rewrites it to use StringBuilder. On Java 9+, it uses `StringConcatFactory` via `invokedynamic` for even better performance. It's only inside loops that you need to manage StringBuilder yourself.

So my rule is: **String for values, StringBuilder for building**, and I haven't had a legitimate reason to use StringBuffer in any codebase I've worked on.
